title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · sec1-p1】Radiomics extracts quantitative features from medical images to characterize phenotypic patterns that may not be apparent through visual inspection alone. PyRadiomics [1] is a widely used open-source Python package whose feature definitions largely follow the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative [2], with documented differences in discretization, resampling, and kurtosis. Radiomics was developed for radiology, where it has been used to study tumor heterogeneity, treatment response, sensitivity to tumor delineation, and integration with genomics [3–6]. It has also been applied to histopathology images, where texture- and intensity-based features have shown clinically relevant patterns [7,8]. In melanoma, Finti et al. recently classified nuclei of the PUMA (Panoptic segmentation of nUclei and tissue in advanced MelanomA) dataset with PyRadiomics and HistomicsTK features [9,10], illustrating both the interest in nucleus-level radiomics and the dependence of such analyses on external Python tooling. On the TIGER (tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in breast cancer) breast-cancer dataset, work has focused on the computational scoring of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes [11], including a QuPath pipeline that segments tumor and tumor-associated stroma before scoring [12].

【Introduction · sec1-p2】QuPath is an open-source platform for whole-slide imaging and digital pathology [13]. It provides cell segmentation, tissue detection, object classification, and measurements of morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture, with extensions for methods such as StarDist and Cellpose [14,15]. A standardized radiomic feature set still requires exporting objects and pixels to external tools. QuRad adds this extraction directly to QuPath for cell detections and annotation regions. We compare its outputs with PyRadiomics under matched preprocessing and aggregation settings, benchmark its throughput, and demonstrate cell- and tissue-level classification. Object identifiers and coordinates accompany the measurements so they can be linked to other spatial data.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Experimental and technical design · sec3-p1】The study had 4 components. We implemented radiomic features as a QuPath extension and an equivalent script; verified their numerical agreement with PyRadiomics on identical pixel masks of a benchmark tile, a second histology dataset, and synthetic images; measured the performance in a reproducible benchmark; and demonstrated their utility by the supervised classification of cells (melanoma; PUMA dataset) and tissue compartments (breast cancer; TIGER dataset) with baseline and ablation models. Figure 1B illustrates the user workflow.

【Software implementation · sec4-p1】QuRad is distributed as an installable QuPath extension and as a self-contained Groovy script that share the same feature-extraction code (version 0.4.0 here). QuRad builds only on QuPath’s Java API and the Java standard library and needs no external plugins or libraries. The extension adds a menu command with a settings dialog and works with QuPath 0.6 and 0.7. The script is opened and run in QuPath’s script editor. Figure 1A gives an overview of the extraction workflow.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Numerical validation · sec9-p1】We used 3 kinds of input. (a) A single breast-cancer tissue-microarray tile (896 × 768 pixels, 410 labeled cells) from the UCSB Bio-Segmentation benchmark [16], whose label image provides a raster ground truth for the masks. (b) The first 20 primary-melanoma tiles of the PUMA training set [17] (ROIs 001 to 020, 1,024×1,024 pixels, hematoxylin and eosin [H&E], 8,649 annotated nuclei). They come from a different scanner and a different tissue, and their polygons are hand-annotated and vary in size and shape. (c) Twenty-five synthetic ROIs on deterministic images (uniform, checkerboard, gradient, 2-level, noise and random-color images). They comprise square, circular, elongated, star-shaped, ring-shaped, sub-pixel-offset, border-touching and border-crossing polygons, ROIs of 1 to 25 pixels, and ROIs of up to 512 × 512 pixels. Table S2 lists them, and for several of them, the feature values are known analytically.

【Numerical validation against PyRadiomics · sec12-p1】Both implementations were given identical inputs, so that only the feature computation is compared. A command-line runner distributed with the source code uses the same calculator as the extension and the script on an image and a set of GeoJSON objects. Its output agrees with that of the extension run inside QuPath (see the “Datasets” section). For every object, it exports the pixel mask it used and the grayscale image it computed. PyRadiomics 3.0.1 was then run on these masks and this grayscale image with the settings of Table 1, with all optional features enabled (firstorder_StandardDeviation, shape2D_SphericalDisproportion, shape_Compactness1/2, and shape_SphericalDisproportion) and with weightingNorm='no_weighting'. A second PyRadiomics run used its default angle aggregation, to measure the effect of this setting. For the benchmark tile, the GeoJSON polygons were traced from the label image with marching squares and shifted by half a pixel into QuPath’s coordinate system. The pixel-center rule must then reproduce the label image exactly. We verified this for every cell, and we verified that the grayscale images computed in Java and in NumPy are identical.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Fig. 1. · F1】Fig. 1. The QuRad workflow. (A) Per-object feature extraction, illustrated on one labeled cell of the breast-cancer benchmark tile: the region of the object is read at full resolution, the polygon is rasterized with the pixel-center rule (orange outline), the pixels are converted to gray levels and discretized with a fixed bin width, and the texture matrices are accumulated over the 4 in-plane directions. The co-occurrence matrix of this object is shown with discretized gray-level bins on both axes, and the bar gives the composition of the 103 features computed by default. Scale bar, 20 μm. (B) The same run as the user performs it in QuPath with the default settings: the image holds the cell detections (blue), the feature classes are chosen in the dialog, every detection is measured, and the values are used inside QuPath, here to shade each nucleus by its mean gray level.

【Fig. 2. · F2】Fig. 2. Application of QuRad features. (A) Three PUMA melanoma tiles (001, 004, and 006, 1,024×1,024 pixels at 0.227 μm per pixel) showing the H&E image, the ground-truth annotations, and the out-of-fold random-forest predictions (tumor = vermilion, lymphocyte = blue, pooled macro-F1 = 0.85 over all 20 tiles). Scale bars, 50 μm. (B) Unsupervised UMAP of the standardized, correlation-pruned QuRad features of a class-balanced subsample of 3,000 PUMA nuclei. (C) Unsupervised UMAP of the 197 TIGER regions (invasive tumor = vermilion, tumor-associated stroma = blue, healthy glands = black). (D) Mean z-scored value per tissue type of the 19 features retained by the correlation filter in every fold, with hierarchical clustering of rows and columns. The bars give the number of regions per class.

【Table 1. · T1】Table 1. Parameters and conventions of QuRad 0.4 and the PyRadiomics 3.0.1 configuration that reproduces them

sections.title: 复现线索
sections.text:
《QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath》：复现时可直接核对的数据、软件或实现线索。

【Data Availability · section-25-p1】The QuRad source code and documentation are openly available at https://github.com/institutducerveau/QuRad under the MIT license. The version evaluated here, 0.4.0, is archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23062835). The repository contains the feature tables of all 3 datasets, the PyRadiomics comparison tables, the benchmark timings, the 3 notebooks and the helper scripts that produce every table and figure panel of the results, and their outputs. The image used for validation is a single breast-cancer tissue-microarray tile from the UCSB Bio-Segmentation benchmark [16], available under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 (CC BY 3.0) license and redistributed with attribution. The biological application datasets are publicly available: the PUMA melanoma dataset [17] from the PUMA Grand Challenge (https://puma.grand-challenge.org/) and the TIGER breast-cancer dataset [18] from the TIGER Grand Challenge (https://tiger.grand-challenge.org/).

【Software implementation · sec4-p1】QuRad is distributed as an installable QuPath extension and as a self-contained Groovy script that share the same feature-extraction code (version 0.4.0 here). QuRad builds only on QuPath’s Java API and the Java standard library and needs no external plugins or libraries. The extension adds a menu command with a settings dialog and works with QuPath 0.6 and 0.7. The script is opened and run in QuPath’s script editor. Figure 1A gives an overview of the extraction workflow.
